Abstract: De-identification of electronic health records (EHRs) is essential to safeguard patient privacy, particularly when such data are utilized for large-scale population studies. To evaluate general-purpose LLMs, we employ a combination of prompt engineering techniques and post-processing strategies aimed at improving the accuracy and robustness of the anonymization process. Abstract: Discontinuous named entity recognition is challenging because clinically meaningful mentions may appear in separated fragments rather than continuous spans. This study aims to develop and evaluate a Large Language Model augmented grid tagging framework for discontinuous named entity recognition in biomedical and clinical text. The methodology uses an experimental quantitative design with contextual LLM embeddings, token-pair grid construction, relation classification and constrained entity reconstruction. The Colab implementation accepts CADEC and ShARe-compatible JSONL data and includes a reproducible prototype corpus when restricted benchmark files are unavailable. The prototype results show that the proposed LLM-grid model achieved 0.884 precision, 0.845 recall and 0.864 entity-level F1, while Fig. 2 shows a discontinuous-only F1 improvement from 0.743 in the grid baseline to 0.798. The study recommends full benchmark replication, implies a reusable biomedical DNER pipeline, and is limited because the included outputs are prototype results rather than final benchmark scores.

Abstract: Medical records are comprehensive repositories of patient health information and an essential tool for physicians to access medical histories. However, drafting medical records is a time-consuming process that contributes significantly to physician workload. Recent advances in Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) have shown strong potential in text summarization, yet most existing approaches rely on offline generation and singleturn interactions, failing to meet the real-time accuracy and user experience requirements of clinical practice. To address these limitations, we propose MedStructGen, a two-stage medical record generation framework that mirrors real-world clinical workflows. Stage 1 employs a simulation driven multiturn patient-physician dialogue model that adaptively refines its questioning strategy based on evolving symptom profiles, ensuring domain-complete diagnostic information capture. Stage 2 employs stage-specific fine-tuned LLMs with stepwise prompt engineering and entity alignment to generate EMRs that are compliant with standards and machine verifiable. This design not only improves contextual accuracy and completeness of information, but also achieves superior structural compliance, enabling seamless integration into Hospital Information Systems. Experiments on real-world hospital datasets demonstrate that our method achieves a 12.26% BLEU-4 improvement over one-stage baselines, with consistent gains in ROUGE and BERTScore. Located in a partner hospital, our system reduces physician documentation time by 1 to 1.5 hours per day, allowing more focus on patient care and personal well-being. The approach is generalizable and requires minimal customization for integration into other healthcare settings.

Abstract: A major challenge in deep learning (DL) model training is data scarcity. In addition to the ChatGPT augmentation, we applied other augmentation techniques, such as easy data augmentation (EDA) and an easier data augmentation (AEDA), to clinical data. ChatGPT comprehended the contextual significance of sentences within the dataset and successfully modified English terms but not clinical terms. The original CHARDAT datasets represent 52 health conditions across three clinical dimensions, i.e., Treatments, Risk Factors, and Preventions. We compared the outputs for different augmentation techniques and evaluated their relative performance. Publication Title: 2024 14th International Conference on Pattern Recognition Systems (ICPRS)
Abstract: In recent years, the intersection of natural language processing (NLP) and healthcare informatics has witnessed a revolutionary transformation. One of the most groundbreaking developments in this realm is the advent of large language models (LLM), which have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in analysing clinical data. This paper aims to explore the potential of large language models in medical text classification, shedding light on their ability to discern subtle patterns, grasp domain-specific terminology, and adapt to the dynamic nature of medical information. This research focuses on the application of transformer-based models, such as Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT), on hospital discharge summaries to predict 30-day readmissions among older adults. In particular, we explore the role of transfer learning in medical text classification and compare domain-specific transformer models, such as SciBERT, BioBERT and ClinicalBERT. We also analyse how data preprocessing techniques affect the performance of language models. Our comparative analysis shows that removing parts of text with a large proportion of out-of-vocabulary words improves the classification results. We also investigate how the input sequence length affects the model performance, varying sequence length from 128 to 512 for BERT-based models and 4096 sequence length for the Longformers.The results of the investigation showed that among compared models SciBERT yields the best performance when applied in the medical domain, improving current hospital readmission predictions using clinical notes on MIMIC data from 0.714 to 0.735 AUROC. Our next step is pretraining a model with a large corpus of clinical notes to potentially improve the adaptability of a language model in the medical domain and achieve better results in downstream tasks.

Author Affiliations: Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, China; Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, China; Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, China; Department of Cardiology, Union Hospital, Key Laboratory for Biological Targeted Therapy of Education Ministry and Hubei Province, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, China; Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, China; Guizhou Communications Polytechnic University, Guiyang, China
Publication Title: 2026 3rd International Conference on Electronic Engineering and Information Systems (EEISS)
Abstract: Coronary artery disease (CAD) diagnosis in real clinical practice requires multi-source evidence integration across heterogeneous modalities, yet existing AI systems remain limited in cross-modal reasoning and workflow-level deployability. To address this gap, we develop Medi-Agent, a clinically aligned multimodal CAD agent that combines LLM/VLM/RAG capabilities within a task-schedulable multi-agent workflow. The framework supports end-to-end processing from image-based report digitization and structured extraction to multi-source evidence fusion, diagnosis and risk stratification, treatment suggestion generation, and longitudinal record management. An internal feasibility evaluation is conducted on a real-world CAD-related case set from a Grade III Class A hospital, covering complete multimodal report chains. Experimental results show promising module-level and diagnostic performance: information extraction success rate 95.37%, file archiving success rate 99.15%, and medical tool-calling success rate 98.76%; overall diagnostic accuracy reaches 94.12%. Stability testing in continuous multi-turn interactions further reports 0% error rate, 0% crash rate, 0% logical confusion rate, and 100% context-maintenance rate. These findings suggest that Medi-Agent provides an interpretable and workflow-compatible pathway for CAD-oriented preliminary clinical decision support, while larger external validation remains necessary.

Abstract: This work presents the development of a prototype aimed at facilitating access to and reuse of public data in the healthcare field, using as a case study the data available on the website of the National Central Institute for the Coordination of Ablation and Implantation (INCUCAI) of Argentina, in the context of organ donation and transplantation in the Argentine Republic. Abstract: Manual digitization of complex medical surveillance forms is inefficient and prone to errors. While Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) offer automated data extraction, sending raw medical records to cloud APIs raises critical privacy concerns under the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA). This paper proposes a secure, privacy-preserving framework that integrates an interactive data redaction module to fully anonymize Personally Identifiable Information (PII) before AI processing. Abstract: Artificial intelligence is entering a new era with the advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs). These models facilitate efficient learning involving varied modalities and tasks such as visual question answering and image captioning. The capability of such models to carry out self-supervised, semi-supervised, and weakly supervised learning methods to integrate computer vision with natural language processing makes them competent to deal with complex tasks such as disease classification and segmentation tasks in images, cross-modal information extraction, and automatic report writing. By means of pretraining on large volumes of data without annotations, such models can work with less labeled data and improve their capacity to generalize to downstream tasks. In the context of the healthcare industry, such models address critical challenges through the integration of data obtained from various medical imaging modalities with external text-based data such as radiology reports. These have led to novel tools that have been optimized to improve detection accuracy and diagnostic processes. This review paper aims to explore the recent advances in the field of medical VLMs spanning from 2021 to 2026. The primary roles include the identification of a taxonomy to classify such models, the analysis of critical data sets essential for the assessment of such models, and the current real-world implementation. This paper also aims to identify challenges and limitations in existing tools to increase their applicability. In addition, this also outlines future pathways to expand the reach and effectiveness of VLMs in medical applications.

Publication Title: 2026 International Conference on Speech, Multimodal and Advanced Communication Systems (ICSMACS)
Abstract: Unstructured medical text from clinical notes, guidelines, scientific literature, and clinical trial records contains rich knowledge essential for advancing biomedical research and clinical practice. However, its heterogeneity, scale, and semantic complexity hinder effective integration, interpretation, and reuse. Knowledge Graphs (KGs) provide a semantic representation that normalizes medical concepts, integrates heterogeneous sources, and supports reasoning for accurate retrieval, decision support, and knowledge discovery. This review surveys peer-reviewed studies published between 2020 and 2025 that apply KGs to medical textual data. The literature is organized along three dimensions: (i) KG construction and enhancement methods, including ontology-driven, data-driven, and hybrid approaches; (ii) application domains, spanning biomedical translation, drug repurposing, diagnosis, adverse drug reaction detection, personalized medicine, and general tasks such as recommendation, question answering, information retrieval, and summarization; and (iii) emerging synergies between KGs and Large Language Models (LLMs) for grounded reasoning, retrieval, and generation. We synthesize methodological trends, datasets, and evaluation practices; provide a consolidated comparison of representative works; and highlight persistent challenges related to uncertainty modeling, interoperability, scalability, and privacy. Finally, we discuss promising directions for developing faithful, interoperable, and clinically impactful KG-based systems for medical text.

To address these challenges, we present an interoperable health information application ecosystem. The proposed solution leverages standards such as HL7 FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) to enable secure and structured data exchange among stakeholders, open-source technologies to reduce costs, and an event-driven microservices architecture to ensure scalability. Author Affiliations: Truman State University, Kirksville, Missouri, USA; Truman State University, Kirksville, Missouri, USA; Truman State University, Kirksville, Missouri, USA; Kirksville Senior High School, Kirksville, Missouri, USA; Kirksville College of Osteopathic Medicine, A T Still University, Kirksville, Missouri, USA; Bemnet Kinfe is with Yale University, New Haven, CT, USA; Department of Anatomy, Kirksville College of Osteopathic Medicine, Kirksville, Missouri, USA; Department of Computer and Data Sciences, Truman State University, Kirksville, Missouri, USA
Publication Title: IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics
Abstract: This review investigates recent advances in machine learning (ML) for drug repurposing, with applications spanning COVID-19, Parkinson's disease, and cancer. We provide a methodological taxonomy of ML techniques including supervised learning (e.g., random forests, SVMs), unsupervised clustering and dimensionality reduction, deep neural networks, reinforcement learning, and graph-based models such as MLGANN and DTD-GNN highlighting their roles in scalable drug–target interaction prediction and phenotype mapping. Case studies demonstrate how integrated models leveraging heterogeneous data (e.g., gene expression, chemical structure, EHRs) facilitated the identification of repurposable candidates like baricitinib, raloxifene, and rapamycin. Across the reviewed case studies, top-performing models achieved AUROC values ranging from 0.88 to 0.99 on their respective benchmarks, though significant performance degradation (AUROC drops of 0.05–0.15) was observed under cross dataset generalization, underscoring the translational gap between benchmark and real-world performance. We analyze computational challenges, including data sparsity, model overfitting, limited generalizability across datasets, and the interpretability gap in deep learning and GNNs. We discuss integration of explainable AI (e.g., SHAP, LIME), interpretable models (e.g., rule lists, causal graphs), network biology, and federated learning as avenues to improve robustness and translational relevance. Unlike prior reviews focused on single diseases or ML paradigms, this work provides a cross disease analysis exposing shared bottlenecks and identifying disease-agnostic best practices. We examine the role of foundation models and large language models (LLMs) in drug repurposing, including zero-shot molecular property prediction and literature-informed mining. This work outlines an ML-driven framework that balances computational scalability with biological validity, enabling actionable predictions in precision medicine.

Abstract: Postoperative complications following hepatectomy for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remain frequent and are associated with increased mortality and healthcare costs. Existing predictive models often struggle with extreme class imbalance and fail to capture the holistic complication burden by treating risks as disjointed tasks. To overcome these limitations, we propose PMCP, a novel Prototype-Guided Multi-task Complication Prediction framework designed to jointly predict the holistic Comprehensive Complication Index (CCI) alongside four specific severe complications within 24 hours postoperatively. PMCP leverages a large language model to distill unstructured clinical narratives, orchestrating an adaptive fusion with longitudinal structured electronic health records to circumvent modality laziness. To counteract majority class suppression, we introduce a dual-prototype mechanism that selectively amplifies rare, high-risk clinical signals and maintains distinct feature space separation. Evaluated on the real-world clinical cohort, our framework significantly outperformed state-of-the-art baselines. PMCP achieved an AUC of 0.800 for CCI, and AUCs of 0.935, 0.798, 0.798, and 0.887 for the four specific complications, respectively. Furthermore, the model exhibited a strong capacity to maintain predictive performance even with 40% missing structured data. In summary, PMCP provides a promising framework for early postoperative complication risk assessment and may support individualized monitoring and intervention planning after hepatectomy.
